summary.heading: Describing motion
summary.html:
• Distance is the total path length (a scalar). Displacement $s$ is the change in position, $s = \Delta x$, measured in a straight line from start to finish (a vector: give a sign or direction).
  • Speed = distance ÷ time (scalar). Velocity is the rate of change of displacement (vector). Both in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
  • Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$. Negative acceleration means it points in the negative direction, not always "slowing down".
  • Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is an acceleration, even at constant speed (for example, moving in a circle: A.2).
  • Average values are taken over a time interval; instantaneous values at one moment (the limit of shorter and shorter intervals).

summary.heading: Motion graphs
summary.html:
GraphGradientArea under it
$s$–$t$velocity(not useful)
$v$–$t$accelerationdisplacement
$a$–$t$(not needed)change in velocity
  • Average value: gradient of the chord between two points. Instantaneous value: gradient of the tangent.
  • Area below the time axis on a $v$–$t$ graph is negative displacement. Distance: add the sizes of the areas; displacement: add them with their signs.
  • A ball thrown straight up (no air resistance, up positive): the $v$–$t$ graph is a straight line with gradient $-g$, crossing zero at the highest point. The areas above and below the axis are equal, because the ball returns to where it started.
  • Non-uniform acceleration is treated graphically and qualitatively: curved $v$–$t$ graph, acceleration = gradient of the tangent, displacement = area (count squares).

summary.heading: Equations of motion (constant acceleration only)
summary.html:
$$v = u + at \qquad s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}$$ $$v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as \qquad s = \frac{(u + v)}{2}\,t$$
  • List the five quantities $s, u, v, a, t$: you need three to find the others. Pick the equation that leaves out the one you don't know and don't need.
  • Don't use them when the acceleration changes: with air resistance, for a mass on a spring, in circular motion (the direction of the acceleration keeps changing) or far from a planet's surface ($g$ gets smaller). Use graphs instead.
  • Choose a positive direction first and keep to it.
  • Free fall (no air resistance): $a = g = 9.8$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$ downwards for all objects, whatever their mass. If up is positive, $a = -9.8$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
  • $g$ can be measured by timing falls from several heights: a graph of $s$ against $t^2$ is a straight line through the origin with gradient $\tfrac{1}{2}g$.
  • Motion can be measured with light gates (speed = length of the card ÷ time the beam is blocked), strobe photos or video against a scale, or a motion sensor and data logger. Several readings plotted on a graph give a more reliable value than one timing.

summary.heading: Projectiles
summary.html:
• With no air resistance, the horizontal and vertical motions are independent, linked only by the time.
  • Resolve the launch velocity: $u_x = u\cos\theta$, $u_y = u\sin\theta$.
  • Horizontally: constant velocity, $x = u_x t$. Vertically: constant acceleration $g$ downwards, so use the equations of motion.
  • At the highest point $v_y = 0$, but the acceleration is still $g$ downwards.
  • For a given launch speed, on level ground with no air resistance, the greatest range is at a launch angle of 45°.
  • The path is a parabola (its equation isn't needed). Know launches horizontally, above and below the horizontal.

summary.heading: Relative velocity
summary.html:
• The velocity of A relative to B: $v_{AB} = v_A - v_B$ (vector subtraction).
  • In one dimension, use signs. In two dimensions at right angles, use Pythagoras and $\tan^{-1}$ for the direction.

summary.heading: Fluid resistance (qualitative)
summary.html:
• Drag acts opposite to the velocity and increases with speed.
  • A falling object: acceleration $g$ at release, then the drag grows, so the acceleration decreases until drag = weight. Then the resultant force is zero and it moves at terminal speed.
  • Projectile with air resistance (compared with a vacuum): lower maximum height reached sooner, shorter range, decreasing horizontal velocity, a steeper descent (not symmetrical), and an acceleration that isn't constant.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Using the equations of motion when the acceleration isn't constant (use graphs).
  • Mixing horizontal and vertical quantities in one equation.
  • Using a chord when the question asks for an instantaneous value.
  • A calculator left in radians when resolving velocities.

Observations: Why did Aristotle's idea last so long? What everyday observations support it, and what was different about Galileo's observations?
Drop a sheet of paper and a book side by side, then put the paper on top of the book. What does each version show, and what does it not show?
Measurement: Compare timing a 1 m fall with a hand stopwatch and with a light gate. Roughly how big is each uncertainty, and could each one tell 9.8 from 9.5 $\text{m s}^{-2}$?
Can a better instrument ever change what we believe, or only make us more confident?
Models: List the assumptions behind the equations of motion. For a thrown ball, a sky-diver and a sprinter, which assumption fails first?
Is a model that is "wrong but useful" still scientific knowledge?

oracy.html:
Opinion line (whole class, 8 minutes): students stand on a line from "agree" to "disagree", then justify their place to someone standing far from them. Claim: "A ball thrown straight up has zero acceleration at the top of its flight, because it stops there."

  • I'm standing here because …
  • I've moved, because …
  • That's true of the velocity, but …

Listen for: the velocity is zero for an instant but still changing, so the acceleration is $g$ = 9.8 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ downwards throughout.

If a model is never exactly right, why t: Ask students to name a situation where they rely on an imperfect model every day (weather forecasts, maps, satnav arrival times).
Who decides what counts as "good enough": the scientist, the engineer or the person using the result?
Should we trust our intuition?: Poll the class before showing the dropped-and-pushed balls (or the MythBusters bullet video). How many predicted correctly?
Is intuition useless in science, or is it where hypotheses come from?
Does it matter if the story is true?: Galileo's Pisa experiment may be a myth. Does a false story about a true result do any harm?
Compare how textbooks and historians tell the story of a discovery. Why might they differ?
Can motion be captured in symbols?: What does a graph or an equation show that a video of the motion doesn't, and the other way round?
Are the equations of motion discovered or invented?
